utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, so much, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon counsel, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all participants in the proceedings. Novak Lukic and Boris Zorko representing Mr. Perisic today in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. You may call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Novakovic. Just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope you had a good rest with this wonderful weather that we have been having in The Hague these days. I'm going to continue where we left off on Thursday last week; that is to say, let's discuss the meeting referred to in 65 ter document number 03382D.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'd like to ask you a question, if it's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you have any questions, you should address the Bench, but maybe first you have to ask for their leave if you would like to address me. Depends on what you are going to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Novakovic, what do you want to ask Mr. Lukic, you can ask. We can only tell you whether the question is permissible after you've asked it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask, or I should have asked you instead of Mr. Lukic, is whether I can give my account of this particular meeting and what is currently on our screens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's put it this way, you are going to answer Mr. Lukic's questions. I think Mr. Lukic knows what account he want to put on the record about this meeting. So just answer his questions and if at the end of his questions you feel you want to add something, let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you a few questions about this meeting and at the end if you would like to add something or clarify something, we are at your disposal. But before we continue where we left off last week, can we please have on our screens, just as a reminder, the document related to the meeting held on the 24th of September, 1993, as recorded in Mr. Mladic's notebook. It was held in the attendance of Mr. Milosevic, General Perisic, yourself, and General Mladic. Let us look at page 3 where we left off last week when we adjourned on Thursday. But before we go on, let me ask you a couple of general questions relating to your meetings with President Milosevic. On the first day of your testimony, you told us briefly that you had quite a few of meetings at the time when you were the commander of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, sometimes those were group meetings or sometimes you met tete-a-tete with the president. Now, I'm interested in the period starting from the date of your appointment as commander of the Army of the Serbian Krajina and let us remind ourselves that was in October of 1992 until September 1993. Over the period of that year, can you remember how frequently you met President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just look at the screen. You have used almost two-thirds of the page just to ask how frequently you met with Mr. Milosevic. I know that you were trying to give background, but this whole background is already on the record. Just try to be brief with your questions, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to make this as a kind of introductory just to remind ourselves what we discussed on Thursday. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that your introduction is very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may answer, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me how many times you met approximately, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those 10 or 11 months, there were some 20 meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what kind of conclusions did you draw from these meetings with President Milosevic? What was his position at the time regarding the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, specifically in Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that on the Serbian side, that is to say both the Serbian side and representatives of the international community that was involved in seeking the solution to this conflict, he was considered to be an absolute authority on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe my question wasn't clear enough. What was your conclusion about his personal attitude, and in view of his position of his function, what was his attitude, was he supportive of the conflict or was he opposed to it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obviously misunderstood your question. I'm glad that you asked me that and I'm going to answer it in the following way: Whenever I went to see Mr. Milosevic I knew in advance that what was to follow was guidance or direction to become lenient and to resort to negotiations. Whenever I saw in the media that a representative of the international community of high authority came to visit, I immediately expected him to invite the leadership of the Serbian Krajina and that after that he would try to explain the need for entering negotiations, and he would even issue directions to start specific negotiations either with the Croatian side or with representatives of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his position at the time, and we talking about the period that I limited to the period from the beginning of your duty until September 1993, how much was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia involved in that conflict, in any sense? What was his position towards this involvement?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the involvement of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, I can say that Mr. Milosevic tried hard to have the FRY involved in the war itself to the least possible extent, whereas as far as diplomat efforts were concerned towards ending the conflict was at its maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in more detail what you have just told us now about the efforts to have the FRY involved in this conflict as little as possible, did that position pertain throughout the whole period or did he change his mind at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you've confined Mr. Novakovic to the period when he was in office from 1992 to September 1993. Now, your question says throughout the whole period, which period? Is it that period or the whole period of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Novakovic, did you continue to meet President Milosevic after you were removed from the position of commander of the Serbian Army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a problem, I heard the translation into English. I hope there won't be any further problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm asking you about the whole period of war from the moment you first met him until the end of war, what was the position of Mr. Milosevic vis-a-vis the involvement of Yugoslavia in the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do have an objection. Well, he says -- well, General Novakovic says he did meet with Milosevic after the period he was the commander, he doesn't say when or how long or during what period of time, so now we jump from the simple answer of yes he did to a question that's very broad. Now he's asked his opinion about his -- the opinion about Milosevic's attitude toward the entire war, and we don't have a sufficient foundation still for that question to be properly answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether we are all on the same wavelength. I understood Mr. Lukic at the beginning of his examination today to limit witness to the period when the witness was in office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He now asked a question about Mr. Milosevic's attitude towards the FRY's involvement in the war during the entire period of the war. And just hold it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I then said to him, Mr. Lukic, you began by saying the witness must tell us about the time when he was in office, now you are asking him about the entire period of the war. Having -- I after asking that question, he then asked the question, did you meet with Mr. Milosevic after you were out of position, after you had been removed from your position. And the witness says yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree with that so far, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then he says, based on the fact that they did meet even after, he is now asking the question of Mr. Milosevic's attitude during the entire period of the war. Unless you are saying they didn't meet at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My objection is this: We've gone part of the way in of getting to the proper foundation. We don't know how many times after General Novakovic became the commander he met with Milosevic. Maybe - and I'm just speculating for the sake of example - he met with Milosevic after he resigned or after he was terminated as the commander of the SVK in October of 1993. He met with him once or twice. The war ended in 1995 in December of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say now. Okay, fine. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is more appropriate to tackle this subject in cross-examination if Mr. Harmon is disputing anything I am asking the witness. All I'm asked him is whether he met him and what his impressions were. I can go into further detail regarding these meetings if you deem this to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true, that Mr. Harmon could go into -- could deal with it in cross-examination, but it's a simple question to put to the witness just how many times did you meet with Mr. Milosevic after you had been removed from office, and he will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you were removed from your position of the commander of the Serb army of Krajina in February 1994 until the end of the war, which I think was marked by the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it February 1994 or October 1993 -- September 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was February 1994. I think Mr. Harmon was mistaken and I think I have given you a more precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was operating, Your Honour, off the answer and the question that was at page 3, I believe, line 16, where he was asked to affirm whether he was the commander from, I think October of 1992 until September of 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- and therefore I think the witness has affirmed that and that's why I made an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Lukic, you are going to have to be consistent with your periods. At page 3 you said: "But before we continue where we left off last week, can you please have on our screens, just as a reminder the document, relating to a meeting held on the 24th of -- I am sorry, that's not it. Right. At page 3, from line 13: "Now, I'm interested in the period starting from the date of your appointment as commander of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, and let us reminds ourselves that was in October 1992 until September 1993." Your actual words, Mr. Lukic. Now you jump into February 1994. Which is the correct one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the whole of my thesis concerning those questions, Your Honours, was to elicit from the witness information about his meetings with President Milosevic before the meeting we are discussing now, and this is why I took the September because it refers to this meeting. Before this point, I did not make references to his dismissal which happened in February 1994. I apologise if I've introduced any [indiscernible] of misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did because you're saying let us remind ourselves that the period of his appointment as commander of the army Serbian Krajina was from October 1992 until September 1993. This is what you are saying in that sentence. It can only have the ordinary meaning of the words used there. Okay. Now, you are saying he was terminated in February 1994, and therefore the meeting that you are now about which you have a document on the screen is a meeting that took place after he had been terminated or before he was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. The fewer words we use, the more precise and succinct we shall be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you did not answer my question. From the moment you were terminated from the position of the commander of the SVK until August 1995 when Operation Storm took place, how many times was it that you met President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you used to meet with him tete-a-tete on occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least once, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to this document, please. Let's take a look at page 3, please. This is where we left off on Thursday. That would be page 3 in B/C/S. I'm going to focus on certain segments that I deem important that you, as a witness, confirm to the best of your recollection in terms of what were the topics discussed. With respect to this page, I'd like to discuss the last sentence or the last entry where it states: "In Krajina (RSK) everything must be placed in a subordinate position." Do you recall President Milosevic being referred to as the author of those words? In what context did he utter those words?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall quite well because I do recall what was the occasion when this sentence was uttered. It was a consequence of different conflicts politicking in the Serbian Krajina answering from -- was a situation where para-military armed formations were being set up. The Main Staff of the SVK reacted to this, and some of those people were brought to account. The basis for such para-military organisations was an idealogical one. Some people thought that we who had been in the JNA were professional -- had been professional officers were not true Serbian officer material. They thought that we were supposed to be more Serb, in a way, and which means that we were supposed to hold more extreme opinions. Mr. Milosevic by saying this was trying, as far as I could understand, to suggest that this could be very dangerous for an otherwise weak defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Babic and Martic, with respect to those units that you referred to a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This rivalry did not stop, that rivalry between the two of them. Sometimes it would go up or down in intensity. It goes with information that the Main Staff of the SVK had at the time we thought that Mr. Martic was behind the attempts to organise some of those para-military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 4, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This entry, the second sentence attributed to President Milosevic: "All plans are to be made as if the war will not stop, and on the political front work to achieve peace." Do these words reflect generally President Milosevic's words to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He could not have said anything else because some ten days before that, Croatian operation in the Medak pocket had been completed where they applied the principle of scorched earth. On the other hand, he held that under those circumstances, and as he put it, we should not escalate the conflict in any way and to focus in Krajina towards achieving peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to skip the following two pages and let's go then to page -- just a sec, bearing page 6, I think, please. That's correct. Let's wait for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These are supposed to be the words of President Milosevic because I do not see anybody else as participating in the conversation. So the first paragraph, General, could you please read for yourself, or should I read it out for everybody's benefit? "We now must achieve the final verification of RS which covers around 28.000 kilometres, and that's the size of two Slovenias. We are effectively one country at this moment, informally ... We must have" and then it states "Pol co-ordination" or political co-ordination, "Lilic, Mil, Kar, and Hadz. Government co-ordination (civilian co-ordination) prime minister without Montenegro, economic co-ordination, political co-ordination of political power." And below that it is stated something that I'm going to ask you something special about, but before that, can you recall what these words reflect, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are President Milosevic's words. I remember them quite well because they reflected, in my opinion, a very important political position. Mr. Milosevic here expresses an attitude that we were effectively politically united, although at that moment for me this was more of a goal or a vision of the future. I would not concede that that was the realistic state of affairs at that time. As far as the final verification of RS is concerned, this refers to the Republika Srpska where he mentions the land area of the RS, at the time 28.000 square kilometres, and warns of something which at the time and later on was problematic among the leadership of the Republika Srpska, and that was that they kept maintaining that in terms of ownership in land registry, two-thirds of land in Republika Srpska was in the hands of Serbs. And this is why he makes this reference about the RS is twice as large as Slovenia. By the same token, my memory allows me to say that this entry, political co-ordination, Lilic, Mil, Kar, and Hadz refers to the president of the FRY, the then president Mr. Lilic; then the president of Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic; president of Republika Srpska, Mr. Karadzic; and president of the then Republic of Serbian Krajina, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further on he thinks that co-ordination should be done at government level first and foremost in economic terms, or in economic affairs, as it's stated here, economic co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a second, please. Let's go on with this, when Milosevic uttered those words and when he said we are effectively one country, did you believe in accordance with your information that he believed that you were effectively one country, and by this I mean, the RS, Republic of Serbian Krajina, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you answer that, can we just look properly at the words used. Mr. Milosevic doesn't use the words "effectively," he used the word "informally," and I think there is a difference between those two. Look at the document on the screen and look at your question, Mr. Lukic. Oh, okay. He does say "effectively" but he says "informally," too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both terms are used in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in the English too, I am sorry, are used in the English too. But I think we mustn't emphasise the one against the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, which means those words as stated that I read out as his words "we are effectively one country at this moment, informally," whether those words really reflected Mr. Milosevic's opinion of the time, when those words were uttered?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that those words more reflected his projections. It was more of something that was supposed to become and that at that moment for us -- for us in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and those in Republika Srpska, those words were supposed to be an encouragement reflecting the fact that he was one hundred per cent behind us. I took that as his intention of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then the final entry on this page: "Military component: (Per M.H.) performed the function of joint GS or Main Staff." I'm reading out those acronyms as stated here. Does this entry trigger any of your memories?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After stating positions on the political co-ordination and co-ordination at the level of the governments as primarily economic business co-ordination, he also stated a position on the need for military co-ordination, and it says military component in parentheses, Perisic, Mladic, Novakovic play role of joint General Staff. As far as I understood it at the time, this was an expression of a political orientation which in the event it was actually implemented could have been a very important thing for us in the Serbian Krajina, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you see the discrepancy here between what was written in the English language and between what the witness just said, and I'm stating my opinion again but I agree with Mr. Harmon that this should go for official translation. The translation service with [B/C/S spoken]. These are two separate words that the witness explained. As you can see, it says here "performed" as something in the perfect tense, and I see that the interpreting service in the booths adequately translated it as "play a role," so not perfect as is stated in the official translation which I believe is quite significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe you might cast light, I'm not sure what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no problem with this passage and other passages that we discussed earlier being submitted to CLSS. The witness, however, was asked to, if this entry triggered any of his memories and his answer deals with what this -- memories were triggered by this particular passage. So there's two separate matters we are dealing with. One is the translation on this page, whether it's correct or not correct, that we'll deal with CLSS, but this witness has given us what memories were triggered as a result of that and that answer is part of our record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. And I really didn't follow Mr. Lukic why suddenly he wants to go to his -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the witness. We are talking about an abbreviated word in the Serbian here, and you cannot see from that abbreviated word whether it's past tense, present tense, or future tense. The translation service translated it in the past, "performed the function of the joint Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So? That's what we've got before us. We have I agreed this is going to go back for retranslation. I am not quite sure why your comment. And you are now commenting on -- you're saying you are going to ask a question and you are commenting before you ask the question, so I'm not quite sure what effect your comment is going to have on the answer that we are going to get, and that's my concern. I would rather get the answer first and then your comment later, if your comment is necessary at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not going to dwell on this any more. We can move on and then the translation service can give its official answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This first entry, General, and we'll see the English version in a minute, is what I'm interested in. And these are also supposed to be the words of President Milosevic where he says: "I have to speak with the leadership of Republika Srpska. They cannot -- they are not to go into some vulgar capitalism. It was not prof. who won the war, but the poor. One cannot speak about any kind of a system which the people will not accept; the people are not to be enslaved by a few of some rich people among them." General, do you remember this entry and do you remember what this referred to that I have just read?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this clearly as well because we are talking about an occurrence that was really very obvious. If you walked or took the road, if you took the road from Belgrade towards Banja Luka, you would be able to see many petrol stations, large catering facilities, restaurants, people with expensive cars, and on the other hand you would be stopped by a fighter from the front asking you if you perhaps had a cigarette or a packet of cigarettes or something like that to spare. This is what Mr. Milosevic is talking about, these kinds of real problems of the accumulation of capital on the part of some people during the war which was something that was quite destructive for army morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will see that these are then still the words, which according to this entry should be the words of President Milosevic. This asterisk at the beginning where it says: "Issue an order to decide who needs to go, and those who refuse must leave the army." That is underlined. Is this something that refreshes your recollection of the words of President Milosevic which are recorded here?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this very well, this position, because as an orientation for me personally it meant quite considerable encouragement. Some several thousand people in the Army of Yugoslavia are referred to here who, up until that time, did not think they should be with their people, with their parents, in a war that nobody asked whether it should be or not and where their place was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say several thousand people in the Army of Yugoslavia, which structure of members of the Army of Yugoslavia are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the officers and non-commissioned officers from the Republic of the Serbian Krajina who originated from there. People who were born in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and those who were born in the Republika Srpska but did not go to that -- to join that army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that later an order was adopted expelling from the army those who did not want to or who refused to go to the Army of the Serbian Krajina or the army? Were there any such cases, let me be more precise, that anyone who refused to go to the Army of the Serbian Krajina or the Army of Republika Srpska was expelled from the army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such case. The official explanation given later was that there was no legal framework for something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page. I am skipping some parts that I consider from the point of view of the Defence are not essential, and we don't have to put questions on those sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is said here, there is a subheading: "Question in the RSK." And I'm interested in all of these entries, but I don't have to read them all. General, are you able to read that or do you need me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think I can read this, this subheading, in the RSK --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, and everything that is written until the end of that page.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A, stopping local break-throughs. B, actions along or behind the lines Croatia. Stop actions. Go for an enemy signature and push this on to the political arena. B, no actions from deep within the area of Croatia unless absolutely necessary, as this mobilises all forces against the RSK. We should not provoke through continuous actions an all-out attack against the RSK." This is an entry that corresponds exactly to what Mr. Milosevic said. It means that it confirms what I said here earlier, that in this period that we are talking about, he was saying that even in the conditions of Croatian incursions, we should not do anything that would lead to an escalation of the conflict. At the same meeting, he was also speaking about a possibility which he felt was realistic, especially after his conversations with Croatian President Tudjman, and you have that somewhere here on one of these pages. That is also noted, that the conflict should and must, and it would be favourable for us, first of all, that it was in our interest, in our best interest, for the conflict to be resolved peacefully and for us to move in the direction of negotiations avoiding the war option.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we can skip the next entry, the next page, and we can immediately go to two pages after this entry. This is also then actually the last page. Sorry, can we look at the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You could see on the previous page, and I don't want us to dwell on that, where you could see "with Cot," what does that remind you of, that entry? But I don't want to dwell on that.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was a suggestion for General Mladic to pay attention in his conversations with General Cot, the commander of UNPROFOR at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And at the time did you also meet, do you recall meeting General Cot then?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had separate talks with General Cot at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This last page, at the top it says, the first sentence: "Prikspar [phoen] on cessation of hostilities." Does this abbreviation mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a continuation, actually, of what we were talking about so far about what Mr. Milosevic said, that again at the end he emphasised that we, that's what the entry says, are for accepting a cessation of hostilities agreement. That is what he said and that absolutely fits in with what he was saying before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if we can now scroll up the document, and the last question that is related to this entry is related to what it says at the end in large letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we scroll the document down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it says as follows: "Joint General Staff - that we are treated as the 4th Army in the RSK, as the 5th or some other ..." What does this entry remind you of, General? What is stated here?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly what this is. This is not what Mr. Milosevic said. It's not a statement by him. This is Mr. Mladic's position that he stated then and that he would put forward quite frequently later. That was his demand, and you can see from what is said, you can see we are to be treated as the 4th Army, this means the Army of Yugoslavia had three armies at the time and he is saying we should be treated as the 4th Army, meaning the Army of Republika Srpska. In the RSK as the 5th or some other, we were more to the west even. And his proposal was for us to be treated as the 5th, or however it would be marked otherwise, army but as part of the joint General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, was this joint General Staff ever set up?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the Serb army of Krajina treated as an army of the Yugoslav Army regardless of any designation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why do you say "unfortunately"?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it had been treated in that way, I suppose that if they came under attack, all the armies would be involved in the defence, not only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you be more precise, attacked who?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the Republic of Serbian Krajina coming under attack, or as you put it, a potential 5th Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence, but before that I think we should have it MFI'd pending a revised translation from the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit MFI D440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we started a bit later today than usual, should I continue now or should we take a break as usual?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think we'll take a break as usual. Take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we for a moment go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we must go in closed session according to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are now in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have on our screens document P372.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting for the document to appear, we saw in the notebook that this meeting was held on the 24th of September, 1993. My question is, do you remember if you had any meetings in those days with General Cot, and if you did, can you tell us where you met with him and what was it that you discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We met in Belgrade. It was in a situation that arose regarding joint efforts that General Cot and myself made in order to overcome the situation that was created to find some sort of solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the document on the screen. I don't know how about others in the courtroom. I can continue. I have a hard copy provided that other participants in the proceedings don't have any problems, but now I hear that General Perisic also cannot see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose it is important for General Perisic to see the document, and if he can't see it, we'll have to wait for him to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please put the B/C/S version on the ELMO. If Mr. Harmon agrees, I just made some notes myself, but if that is all right, I think we can use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a clean copy I can give. I think it might be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even better still.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's two-sided, so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters also don't have the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters also don't have the document on the screen. Now, if it's on the ELMO, will the interpreters be able to see it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we can. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you can see this document on your screen. I will discuss it very briefly because I think it's self-explanatory. My first question is, according to what you can remember, were you alone with General Cot on this occasion or were you accompanied by someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met General Cot on that occasion by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I don't have a copy in front of me, can we just scroll down and look at item 4, which is actually a description of the document referring to the meeting with you. And I'm going to read only one sentence and then ask you to comment on it. "General Novakovic" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do so, can we get clarification. General Novakovic says he met Cot alone this time. The heading says meeting with General Perisic, Mladic, and Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this document has a subtitle which says "meeting with General Perisic, Novakovic, and Mladic in Belgrade on the 25th of September." Now, I'm asking you were these persons, i.e., General Perisic and General Mladic present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat again that I had a separate meeting with General Cot. Why this is written as it is in this report, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then it must be another meeting. Because you if you look at paragraph 3, it actually says "General Perisic did not discuss substantive issues, he only mentioned the violation of Yugoslavia's air space," so he certainly was present there. According to this minute. Maybe you got to put another exhibit on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I would like to put a question to the witness. Perhaps if we turn to page -- or rather, item 5, and then perhaps you will have the same impression about this document that I have gathered. Because item 5 reads: "During a meeting with General Mladic," and I'm not going to comment on this in front of the witness, but I believe that in this respect this report speaks about a completely different issue. Not about a joint meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you are -- you are now commenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the witness gave us an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, did you attend a meeting with General Cot in the presence of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you followed my question and the witness's answer, I think that it's now clear what the witness's position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, just a brief comment what is written here about your meeting with General Cot, and it says that in a conciliatory tone, General Novakovic expressed a desire to have the problem of the entry by the Serbian police into the Medak pocket resolved as soon as possible. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but I don't have the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you look at item 4, it says -- can you see this?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it in English, but not in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I'm going to read it out to you: "General Novakovic going back to the current problems in Krajina in a conciliatory tone expressed a desire to have the problem of the entry by the Serbian police into the Medak pocket be resolved quickly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps to assist the witness, we have a spare copy in the Serbian language, if the usher could give this to the witness, it might facilitate the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. I have two corresponding copies and everything is perfectly clear. The sentence that you quoted refers to the implementation of one segment of the agreement that I signed on behalf of the Serbian side, and General Stipetic on behalf of the Croatian side through mediation of Generals Cot and General Pellnas. One of the provisions contained in this agreement was for the sides or the parties to withdraw to their initial positions, at which point this zone would be re-entered by the Serbian police which was guaranteed by General Cot. And that is something that he told me that he will support this with his word of a general. However, having in mind realistical ability of General Cot, who I highly appreciated as an officer, I realised that he didn't have the required strength to implement which was one of the elements in the agreement. And I didn't want to put him personally in an awkward position because I saw that he couldn't resolve that and that he couldn't exert pressure to have it resolved. I don't think that was a realistic option for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask, you were interpreted as having signed this segment on behalf of the Serbian side. Did you sign on behalf of the Serbian side or the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do have a copy in the archives. I'm sure there is a copy of that agreement somewhere. I cannot state precisely whether I was referred to as the signatory on behalf of the Serbian Krajina or a signatory on behalf of the Serbian side. My memory tells me that was done on behalf of the Serbian side. The UNPROFOR and the international intermediaries usually used terms such as parties to the conflict, the Serbian side, the Croatian side, and Croatia authorities, and Serbian authorities in Knin. Those were the most frequently used terms. To the best of my recollection, the wording was "the Serbian side" and the "Croatian side" in this agreement, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your official designation at the time was that of commander of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but because of different perceptions of our status, the difference between how we saw it and how the Croatian side saw it, sometimes those official designations were dropped so that those formalities would not become stumbling blocks and prevent the resolution of the merits of each particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Novakovic. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm done with this document. We may go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry, I was talking to the Registrar when you asked to go into open session. May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should consult with the secretariats. I should go into another set of documents, a voluminous set of documents, and we could use e-court. For instance, the next exhibit I intend to discuss has 15 pages. It's a P exhibit, so I'm not sure how again to proceed, without e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you able to proceed with that exhibit using the ELMO? If you are not, we will have to take an adjournment and we are told by the technicians that it will take them 30 minutes to correct the problem, so you can break for 30 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer we continue working. If Mr. Harmon should tell us whether P2175 is something they have in this courtroom, a clean copy, that would greatly aid us because my copy has been annotated heavily. My learned friend says that they have one, so we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, General Novakovic, we are going to broach another subject. Does the term "co-ordination meeting" mean anything to you and what do you understand that term to mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this meeting that we discussed, the one that took place on the 24th of September, a practice was established whereby once a month representatives of the Main Staff of the SVK and the General Staff of the VJ would hold an official meeting which we labelled "co-ordinating meeting" or "co-ordination." If there are documents pertaining to those meetings, to those conferences, then you would be made aware of the tone which was very characteristic of those meetings, that it was identical throughout at all such meetings to wit we would be requiring, asking matters to be resolved, some of them would be resolved, but most of them would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who took part in those meetings? I'm asking you generally.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the part of the VJ General Staff, Chief of Staff would attend those meetings together with his assistants, as far as I could judge. I did not know the positions of everybody in the room. On the part of the SVK, initially I took part and my assistants, and later on I let Chief of Staff General Djokic to take part in those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you let your chief of general or Main Staff General Djokic to take part in those meetings? Generally, do you recall how many such meetings you attended and what was the reason you stopped attending them and he then started in your place?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I attended the first two or three meetings. After that I delegated that to the Chief of the Main Staff. The reason was quite simple, basically we would be repeating our request and those requests kept being unheeded, and therefore I concluded that those meetings were not of import because they were not beneficial to us. But I pointed this my finger at the screen, indicated my inability to follow the speed of the transcript and interpretation. I'm not sure whether I was too slow or too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Rest assured, the interpreters will let you know if you are speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you this question, Mr. Novakovic, simply because you said you delegated your Chief of Staff. Who was the chief of the staff of the VJ at the time? You said on the part of the VJ General Staff, the Chief of Staff would attend. Who was the Chief of Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Perisic. He was the Chief of General Staff of the VJ. And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in the SVK, what was your official designation? Commander of the Main Staff? And General Perisic was not called commander of the General Staff, he was called Chief of the General Staff? But he was at the same level as you, not at the same level as your subordinate? You were the highest military officer in the army of the SVK, he was the highest military officer in the VJ? You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's correct, General Perisic was the highest-ranking officer in the VJ. And I was the highest-ranking officer in the SVK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we are going to discuss the Law on SVK. We are going to broach those subjects, but not for very long. I'm not sure whether we should go into details for the purposes of this trial. I can see that we have the document I requested on the screen. Thanks to the technical support. General, I requested P2175, a Prosecution exhibit to be brought on the screen. This is page 1 of that document. It is a multi-page document. I'm going to dwell on certain segments. Could you please read what is stated here and tell us whether you remember what was the reason for its generation, what was the issue discussed here since you are indicated as the author of the document.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document it is stated Republic of Serbian Krajina, Main Staff of SVK --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do not read it out loud. The date is the 30th of September. Could you please tell us the reason for you drafting this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you saw, at the 24th of September meeting we concluded that co-ordination meetings should be initiated and six days after that meeting I request from the General Staff of the VJ to set a date for such a co-ordinating meeting to be held between the Main Staff of the SVK, Main Staff of the RSK, and the VJ, and I proposed that this be held in the latter part of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document appears and disappears from the screen. Since we have a hard copy, we better proceed with the help of the ELMO. Let's go now to page 5 in the B/C/S. Let's place it on the ELMO. In English that would be page 0630-5895ET.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in, General, is the document dated the 15th of October, 1993. I can see that you signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for placing this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this document, could you please comment?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is a proposal of issues that agreement should be reached at those meetings that we labelled co-ordinating meetings. As you can see, the document states issues, analysis, and implementation of tasks and missions during the month, assessment of the enemy, results of combat operations of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read it out loud. I believe that the document speaks for itself. What I'm interested in is what is stated are issues, use of directives, et cetera. My question is, at the time did you have your plan of utilisation of the SVK and documents pertaining to that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we had. The plan had been prepared and every army should have a plan of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is stated here a little below: "Elements of joint operations of 11 VK [as interpreted] and 12 K VJ and 11 K SVK." What did this refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the eastern part, which is dislocated in the Baranja and in Western Slavonia and Eastern Srem, we had our 11th Corps stationed there of the Serbian Krajina, and on the other bank of the river Danube, the 12th corps with headquarters in Novi Sad of the VJ. We thought that if two such operative groups were -- whose areas of operations are contiguous, then everything concerning their missions and tasks in that area, that they should be in a way co-ordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this ever come to life, this joint actions and joint activities of the 12th Corps of the VJ and the 11th Corps of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question has to be broken down into two parts. As far as joint actions through plans, that was partially achieved. As far as practical joint actions in the combat zone or the theatre of the 11th Corps, that did not materialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are going to dwell on that subject a bit later. Slightly below it is "stated communications issue, problems of setting up of digital communication system with RS and FRY." Did you discuss this matter and did this digital communication system ever come to be?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not established because allegedly there were no funds to set it up. The same as in the case of the preceding task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I ask you whether it was set up, I know the answer, we know that you were the commander until February 1994 after your dismissal and until the end of the war, whether in that period, did this digital communication system -- was it established or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it has never been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you know that if you had been dismissed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that would bring about such a huge change that the people who were in the army at the time would definitely have informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So because they didn't inform you that, you then say that it didn't happen? Is that the basis for you saying it didn't happen, because they didn't tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time the Yugoslav Army, and I know that for sure, Your Honours, did not procure such communication systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am aware of that, Mr. Novakovic. But I ask you to please listen my question and answer my question. My question is, are you basing your answer that it never happened even after you left on the fact that nobody informed you that it happened because you say it would have brought such a huge change that they would have told you. Now, they didn't tell you, and is that the basis for you saying it didn't happen? You can say yes or you can say no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I wasn't privy to this directly but that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, you are making an assumption that it didn't happen. And I'm not suggesting it did happen, I am just saying -- I just want to be sure that your testimony is either based on factual knowledge on your part or on an assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I left my post, I maintained very good relations with various officers including communications officers, and I'm quite sure that they would have been so delighted about something like that happening, they would have told me definitely. On the other hand, I still continued to use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat your answer. Listen to my question. I'm just wanting to make sure that your answer is based on assumption and not on fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tried to say one more sentence in my previous answer and that is that I continued to use this communications system. And at the end stations of this system, I used to spend a lot of time at Petrovo Gora where there was one such station and I know until the end of the war all the obsolete equipment was still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean by this communication system? Do you mean the co-ordinating meetings? Because this is the co-ordinating meetings at which you came to know that you are not able to get the assistance you required, so when you say you continued to use the communication system, what is that communication system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the existing communication system that I found in place when I took over my duty, and that was an analogue system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose if I persist we'll spend the rest of the day arguing on this point, so I hand you over to Mr. Lukic. Maybe there's something I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, as a follow-up in connection with this topic, can you please tell us what post did you hold after your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called deputy, some called it assistant, of the supreme commander for national security and international relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the light of that post, did you know what the financial material situation of the Army of the Serbian Krajina was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fully, and by that I mean I didn't receive any official reports. However, as for some basic information relating to the resources available, I was definitely privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the communications system of the SVK one of the resources that was of vital importance for the functioning of the army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now move to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while we're on this document before we turn to a different part of this document, just to correct the record, on page 32, line 18, Mr. Lukic was reading from this document the portion that he quotes elements of joint operations and then there is inserted in here, perhaps by error, of 11 VK, and 11 VK does not appear in the document itself, it appears in the transcript only. So there is an error in the transcript, and I want to just direct counsel's attention to that and the Court's attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I accept that. It's probably due to a mistake and of course the original document is in evidence, and I agree with this objection by Mr. Harmon which contributes to us avoiding any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let us move a few pages forward, namely page 9 in B/C/S, and there's a title of this document which says "Issues to be Discussed Through Co-ordination at a Meeting to be Held on the 19th of October 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last four digits in B/C/S are 5899.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, General, there's mention here of the date 19th of October, 1993. Can you tell us the names listed underneath are members of which armies? This may sound as a trivial question, but I need an answer for my next question.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one side we have members of the General Staff of the VJ and on the other side we have the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we move to the next page, Your Honours. The English version says "Issues to be Discussed at Co-ordinating Meeting on the 21st of October 1993." I don't have it in front of me, I don't know if you can follow this in English. It should be 0630-5859 most probably -- 00. 5900ET.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a document which contains questions to be discussed on the 21st of October, 1993, and below towards the bottom of the page you can see the list of the attendants, and I'm again asking you, the members of which armies are cited in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have members of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army on the one hand and members of the Main Staff of the Serb army of Krajina on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see two different dates. I would like to ask you if you remember whether these co-ordination meetings with one of the armies were joint meetings or were they held separately?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those meetings were always held separately. There was never a meeting which we attended alongside the officers of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and with the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page -- actually, to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, we have items to be discussed at the meetings by both staffs on the 23rd of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN page, Your Honours, is in English 063055902 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, there are several subjects listed here, and I would like to have the document scrolled down, or rather, let's skip this, I don't think these things are so important. I'm sorry, General. It says on this page what should be done and how it should be done if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please repeat the question slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic, the interpreters request that you repeat the question slowly. They didn't hear your full question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this document which is "Topics for a Discussion." That's the title of the document. In one of sub-items it says "what should be done and how if 50.000 men are dispatched from NATO?" According to you, what was all this about?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about an estimation and a possibility for the UNPROFOR mandate that had already been deployed in our territory be substituted by a peacekeeping mission. There was a realistic possibility for NATO coming to this area with a peacemaking mission. That is to say that they would be entitled to use force in the areas where they assess was necessary and against the party that they decide should be treated by force. All of this was centred about seeking a resolution for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please now turn to page 14 in B/C/S in electronic version, and the English designation is 0630-5902STR3. There's a title there, "Personnel Issues." Page 3 in English. It's all right now, I can see it's on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you see this in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's a subtitle here which says "Problems" and there are several bullet points. Would you please read it to yourself and tell me everything you know about this particular entry?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we made it sufficiently clear at the beginning. These are the topics that had been prepared for General Perisic by his office staff and he was supposed to impart those topics to representatives of the SVK and the Army of Republika Srpska. Under this subtitle "Problems," the first bullet point refers to "the dispatch of officers born in RSK and RS - difficult to achieve (high ranks)." Mr. Lukic, would you like me to go on reading and commenting on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You need not read all this. Can you just comment on the facts, that is to say, whether everything that is stated here about these problems, does that reflect the factual situation as you knew it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is stated here was known to me as the explanations that were given by the VJ General Staff. However, I cannot say exactly that I found that to be acceptable. It says here that in the Serb army of Krajina there were fewer than 1.000 commissioned and non-commissioned officers, that these officers, when they came to our areas, were complaining about being ill-treated by the local population, that they in the VJ did not know exactly where everybody was deployed because there was no specific organ that was dealing with the dispatch of these officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, you can proceed. Let me just ask an additional question. What you said that the citizens of the RS and RSK did not treat the officers in there properly, can you tell us what exactly you meant by that, although you said something to that effect on Thursday as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It goes for non-commissioned officers and commissioned officers who were born in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The common people resented openly without mincing words that it wasn't fair of them as people who had been trained for war to hide somewhere in Belgrade, whereas your common peasant was manning the front line and that they were coming there only when they had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When they had to, what do you mean by this phrase?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they are coerced to come for a period of time, for a couple of months somewhere, and to return as quickly as possible, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whether their refusal to be seconded, did it bring about any consequences in the VJ to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions there were such consequences. There were occasions where people were called up to fill 10 to 15 buses and they were supposed to muster up at a certain location in Belgrade, and the number of people showing up could not fill a single bus, but no measures were taken against such people who failed to show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go to the next page, Mr. Novakovic, a few questions. What does the abbreviation AVL stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, which acronym?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under problems, second bullet, and clear positions on the status of AVL." What is AVL? Oh come on, now they've changed the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that. This is an acronym, AVL, denoting active-duty military personnel, refers to professional commissioned and non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we please go back to that page. Thank you. And what does CL mean? Oh, civilians. Okay. So this is the same bracket as civilians. Okay. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me speed up since, as you can see, this document contains several subdocuments. Now, I'd like to deal with a portion which would be on page 23 in B/C/S and in English that would be 0630-5913ET. That would be the rear guard sector. That would be the heading. This is a four-page document. However, I'm -- well, I believe that we have this in e-court and hopefully there will be no longer any need for ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph concerning possibilities of the VJ to provide rearguard support to the VRS and SVK, and then the technical support, please read this whole paragraph for yourself, General, and then I'm going to ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, derived from the contacts with the representatives of the General Staff of the VJ, where did those facts particularly in the latter part of the paragraph correspond to the actual state of affairs in terms of the rear guard sector of the VJ at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the only sources of my knowledge would be what I was told by General Perisic and his assistants. I had no reason to believe otherwise either then or now. For instance, they say here: "We have nothing but what is no longer useable by the VJ, which has no perspective of being used there. We can give you those. If you've got the funds, you can buy for yourself if you need anything else."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you procure anything of the sort? And if so, how you secured the funding for such procurement?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with procurement. The Ministry of Defence and the government dealt with that, the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And as far as I know, they gave oil from the Djeletovci oil fields and converted that into funding for fuel and other supplies. Alternatively some funds, most probably money printed by the national bank, was received from the government of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After 1993 in 1994, is it known to you after this Avramovic programme had been introduced, the so-called Avrams dinar, did you receive any such funds coming from the central banks print shop? Is it known to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist of the monetary reform as far as I could understand it was to stop printing money without foreign currency backing, so it was no longer possible for you to print money and say go buy something with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Djeletovci oil fields, where are they, those oil fields, what facilities were there, and what was it all about concerning the Djeletovci agreement or agreement concerning Djeletovci?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited that area once when I visited the front line towards the enemy lines. What I know of that is that in that area there was an oil field controlled by the government of the Serbian Krajina. And I know there was talk about arrangements whereby as far as I know Pancevo refinery would receive crude oil and in return the Pancevo refinery would give oil derivatives to the RSK or funds for procuring something else. I also know that the government, in an effort to deal with the financial issues, in the eastern part of the RSK, they organised some timber felling. There were rumours flying around that as well. But to the best of my knowledge these were the methods to obtain the necessary funding that were used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you where those -- this equipment and supplies were obtained from, so who did they buy when they were buying from?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manufacturers in Serbia who manufactured those necessary items.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here under 3, item 3, it is stated: "VJ has no other possibilities of supplying RSK and SVK with fuel because the reserves are below the statutory minimum. Therefore, supplies have to be obtained -- further supplies have to be obtained from the market." General, what do you know about those facts? Did you as the SVK receive oil and fuel from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was anything before this document, but after that for sure nothing else came. They themselves did not have enough fuel to meet their every-day daily minimum requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm through with this document and since I'm conducting this examination of Mr. Novakovic in a chronological order, I would like to go to another document. I'm going back to General Mladic's notebook. Let us -- first I would like to seek leave from the Bench to introduce into the 65 ter Defence list something referring to a meeting in Belgrade and that would be 03383.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel repeat the date of the meeting, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you repeat the date of the meeting, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 21st of October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon do you have any objection to that being introduced to the 65 ter list of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Yes, Mr. Lukic, it is so introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's bring to the screen this entry from the notebook. That would be 65 ter 03383D. This entry is slightly shorter than the previous ones. We'll be able to go through it faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's stated here: "Meeting with the representatives of the FRY, Serbia, and Republic of Serbian Krajina." Those attending the meeting are Lilic, Slobo, Karadzic, Perisic, Mladic, and Novakovic. The date is the 21st of October, 1993. General, do you recall attending this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My first question, as we can see, the president of the Republika Srpska, Karadzic is presents here, but I can't see anybody else representing the civilian authorities of the Serbian Krajina, Republic of Serbian Krajina. Wasn't it unusual for you to be the only representative of the RSK? What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state unequivocally. Maybe it was a political message to those political leaders of ours to stop the political bickering that occupied the whole time and to focus more on problems.
