utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object. This calls for speculation. I object to the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You should object to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I should have. Once I realised -- once I could see that the witness was speculating, then I was a little bit tardy, but I nevertheless assert my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept Mr. Harmon's objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could that be a convenient moment? We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Saxon. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The e-court now is working fully, I hope. And I would just like us to look at the bottom of this document, of this page. We can begin with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First thing that it says at the end of this first page about this meeting, says next: "Status questions of officers (resolved)." General Novakovic, has this entry reminded you perhaps of what this referred to? We don't see who wrote it. Can you tell us anything about this entry?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the status issue of officers should be looked at. The officers and non-commissioned officers of the former JNA who are currently serving in the Serbian army of the Krajina and the Army of Republika Srpska. Until that time there was some different problems relating to their status, and we requested that these matters be resolved in such a way as to first define the political will to resolve this matter. And this could only be resolved only in this way, at the political level. If you wish, I can list these status issues that made up the bulk of these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides the fact that often they didn't know who was where, the officer who did not have the military post number entered in his medical booklet, military post in the territory of the Republic of Yugoslavia, he could not ask for medical assistance in military medical facilities. What was even more important was that the members of his family, his children, were not able to seek medical assistance if they did not have their medical ID cards certified in the proper way. The next question, for example, is that such an officer or non-commissioned officer couldn't buy a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we already discussed some of those problems that you were facing before, if you remember. I would like to put the question to you, do you remember at that meeting what was the conclusion, if there was a conclusion adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the conclusion by Mr. Milosevic that this status issue should be resolved, and it should be that they have equal status regardless of which members of the former JNA were in the Army of Yugoslavia or the Army of the Serbian Krajina or the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention for the transcript, Your Honours. On page 46, line 18, the witness said in the Serbian Army of the Krajina and the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Instead of "in" you want "and."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, both in the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you, General, for one -- well, I'm not going to say comment, but testimony on another of the entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a problem again here with the official English translation by CLSS, and I have already talked about this with Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to read this part in -- listed under number 2 and you can tell me, General, if I've read it correctly: "The financing of the army. What the VRS RJ has it will give, a share of the materiel we will have to obtain." General, who does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Novakovic, the translation says: "What the VRS RJ has it will give. A share of the materiel we will have to obtain." But I thought it says "what the Army of the FRY have, they will give." Look at page 48, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It's possible -- well, the title was a little bit different. I'm going to say it again: "Financing of the army. What the Army of the FRY has ..." Literally that is the name given, the term Army of Yugoslavia is not used this time. It will give, and a part of the funds or means or equipment we will obtain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember who said this and what does this entry refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are also the words of Mr. Milosevic and that's how it was said, what the Army of Yugoslavia has it will give and a part of the materiel we will obtain from those who produce it, I assume, and what the army doesn't have. If you wish, I can say how I understood this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. This is what I would like you to do.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Army of Yugoslavia is concerned, what this practically meant was that they would not give us anything because they didn't have anything. This is what they told us. Only something that they didn't really have much use for, that is what they would give because they didn't have enough for their own elementary needs either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When Mladic says here "we will have to obtain this," what is he thinking of? What does he mean here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll object to what is he thinking, Your Honour. That calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not asking the witness to speculate. Perhaps the question is formulated in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But could the witness based on what Milosevic said tell us to whom does this part about obtaining things refer to? Who is it that was supposed to obtain these things?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was very important for me and that is why I remember clearly that this meant that as far as I was concerned, the government of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina would have to care about getting those funds, and if we are talking about the government of Republika Srpska, that would imply their Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose Ministry of Defence, let us be precise?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence, as I said, of Republika Srpska, and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I apologise, but perhaps I'm a little bit too fussy somewhere. But I would like to draw your attention to the last part on this page where it says "questions" and underneath that it says "Milosevic." Now, again I'm going to read this out because again I have a problem with the official translation. What is says is this: "The RS is under a significant threat. A couple of units were transferred to Lika from Eastern Slavonia, but we cannot man these forces from Eastern Slavonia." General, who transferred the units, do you remember, from Lika to Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a different translation in the English from what was read. I have the RSK is under a significant threat, and what was translated at page 50, line 9, it says the RS is under a significant threat. So there seems to be a difference in both what was read and what is in the text. Perhaps that can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Obviously this refers to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, so I agree with this objection by Mr. Harmon in any event that that is what it should state in this place, page 50, line 8, RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, does this remind you of the conversation on this topic at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the assessment by Mr. Milosevic that the Republic of the Serbian Krajina is under significant threat. I recall that this was about a month after the incursion of the Croatian forces in the Medak pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I'm asking you what it says here, who transferred a couple of units from Lika to Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one transferred these units from Lika to Eastern Slavonia. Actually, it's the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I think I'm getting a bit tired myself.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the Serbian Army of the Krajina transferred two battalions from the 11th Corps from the eastern sector to Lika because people there had been at positions for over a month without any relief, without the possibility of going home, having a bath, resting, doing something else. If you would like me to continue with my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, for reasons unknown to me, said that this should not be done, this transfer of units which are units of the Serbian army of the Krajina. They should not be transferred from the 11th Corps area in the eastern part to Lika where the incursion into the Medak pocket was carried out. What he is saying is that Boric and Talic should give them assistance amounting to some 3- to 5.000 men in that area. General Boric at the time was the commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska. And General Talic was the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska. And Mr. Milosevic, and I know this very well, I mean, it was a bit unclear to me, fought or suggested that they should provide these men. And they did send a battalion each to relieve these other units, but not 3- to 5.000 men as it is stated here. They just didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the next page, please. This is a continuation of this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the first sentence says: "By October 27th, 1993, two brigades, about 3.000 men to be given to the RSK to Lika." My question is, and you have just said that, is members of which army went to Lika, if any went at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went from the 1st Krajina Corps of General Talic and the 2nd Krajina Corps of General Boric, about 500-strong battalions each from these corps was sent to certain parts of the front so that those people from the Serbian Army of Krajina could be relieved and could rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. Just so that at least we follow you, this entry tells us of something that is to be done. The witness is testifying about something that was done, sending 500 each from each of those corps, and he is using the past tense but this entry talks about the future, to be done. To be given to the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question to the witness, in fact, was occasioned by this entry and I wanted to ask whether at a later stage -- let me just check whether the question was recorded properly. If you look at page 52, line 9, it says whether anything was done later in compliance with this entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, General, do you remember how long they stayed in the area and what happened afterwards? I am talking about these two battalions.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between three and four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to whose decision did they return to the VRS and what happened with them subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no decision taken subsequently. At the time when they were dispatched, it was said that they would stay there about one month to give an opportunity to our men to rest and that after that they would return to their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now, could you please look at what is written next underneath the previous statement, and it reads -- it says here VSRJ, and I suppose that this refers to the army of the FRY, it says: "Call all officers and non-commissioned officers from the army of the FRY by the end of the next week," and then there's an arrow. And it says: "Officers are to go to the VRS and the VRSK." General, based on this entry, can you remember what was discussed on that day, what does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was said by Mr. Milosevic as well. And it was a kind of declaration that he made, but he didn't mean it in actual fact. If necessary, let me remind you that among the topics prepared by Mr. Perisic's office staff for a meeting with us, it was said that this was not feasible, that that could not be done because there was no legal basis for such a move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you know whether at that time before or after there were any rallies organised where officers and non-commissioned officers were invited together?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these kind of rallies were organised within the Army of Yugoslavia and by them, and at these rallies, they were reminded of their moral obligations first and foremost, and I myself did not attend any of such rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any feedback information about the reaction by the officers who were called to go to and join the Army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, Mr. Lukic, I did not dwell too much on their reactions. I was rather interested to see what the response was and it was negligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be given an exhibit number and for the time being I would like it to be marked for identification only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You Honour, that will be MFI D441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last document that I would like to go through with this witness relating to this particular format, that is to say, General Mladic's notebook, is an entry from the meeting held on the 8th of November, 1993, at the Presidency of Serbia, and on our 65 ter list, it is marked 03384D. I'm just waiting for Mr. Harmon to hear what he thinks about including this into our list, and then I would like to go through it with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this is a multi-page document and it speaks about a meeting at the Presidency of Serbia. As you can see stated here it was held on the 8th of November, 1993, in Belgrade. Do you remember -- but before that, during proofing have I shown you this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this document refresh your memory concerning this meeting and your presence in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. We have the full leadership of the republic of the Serbian Krajina present here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just identify only a few of the participants who are listed here. I will skip Milosevic and Lilic. Tell me who Sainovic is?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the prime minister of Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have Perisic, then Sokolovic. Who was Sokolovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time Sokolovic was the minister of the interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stojsic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of public security in the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic was the chief of the state security department of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since there's another Stanisic mentioned here, do you know his first name, the one that attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have Karadzic, Krajisnik, Mladic, Hadzic. Who was Hadzic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bjegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djordje Bjegovic was the prime minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have Martic and Novakovic. We mentioned that before. Who is this person Rakic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Rakic was the minister of defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say Sainovic was the president of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't understand you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say Sainovic was the president of Serbia, did I hear you to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Lilic was the president of the Federation -- FRY and Milosevic was the president of Serbia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at -- first we have a contribution by Milosevic who -- I'm going to speak this, and it says: "Today's agenda, important element of policy and military strategy, current situation." I would like to skip this whole part because I think this document is self-explanatory in this particular segment, and I would like to move on to the next page. Somewhere in the middle there is mention of the leadership of the Serbian Radical Party and the SPO. In your view, why was it important for Milosevic to mention these political parties that existed at the time as part of the political system of Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was known to everyone, to all members of the public was that at the time in Serbia there was fierce political fighting between the position and opposition. At that time, the fiercest conflict was between the socialist party of Serbia, led by Mr. Milosevic and who was in power on the one hand, and the Serbian Radical Party on the other led by Mr. Seselj. Our assessment was that the mention of these issues in a meeting with the political leaderships of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina by Mr. Milosevic signified that he was actually seeking political support from us for maintaining and preserving his political position in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I explain now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. May the Chamber please move into private session. And could we please redact that portion starting at page -- line 18 of page 57 up to page 58, line 8.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, let's work through this document. These words are also Milosevic's, and it is stated: "Our objective: First, unconditionally strengthen the integrity of Serbia. 2, set up RS as a completely independent state. 3, in the RSK, the Serbs must have complete power." I would like you to testify about your recollections of what this entry refers to.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important to notify the nuances here because they are important when we talk about those items 1, 2, and 3, because they represent the gist of the whole issue, and this is how I understood them at the time. First of all, unconditionally strengthen the integrity of Serbia. In effect, we are being told that only a politically stable Serbia could be something we could rely upon and that would be a Serbia where in the SPS is in government without any serious challenges to that power. Second item, set up RS or the Republika Srpska as a completely independent state. That is a request to the military and political leadership of Republika Srpska to be satisfied with what they've got, and that they should strive towards something which would mean making progress towards peace and acceptance of the RS on the part of international actors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Acceptance in what form?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And item 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, let's just set up RS as a completely independent state, in light of your answer, in what form should the international community accept Republika Srpska? What was Milosevic's stance on that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is jotted down here is "as an independent state." I did not remember that as such. I remembered it as a state. I believe, to the best of my recollection, this was jotted down by Mr. Mladic as an independent state, but I understood it to be a state, some entity, which has fought for its acceptance and that, as such, it should be accepted by international community and actors, and for me that was the most important -- what was the most important thing for me was under item 3. The gist of this entry is -- corresponds to the gist of what Mr. Milosevic said at the time, in the RSK, the Serbs must have complete power. Serbs in the Republic of Serbian Krajina were a majority. They would be a majority if -- even if all the refugee Croats and others were to return, which would be desirable for the RSK, but here Mr. Milosevic does not state that it should become a state, and this is something which I noticed. I noticed that difference. I'm not sure whether other participants in the meeting from the RSK noticed it, but this was an important difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next sentence, let's discuss it, please: "The basic precondition: Confront the strategy of exhaustion with a strategy of offensive initiative. Prove to the US," SADs, but you'll confirm whether this stands for the US, "that their policies in the Balkans are pro-German..." Now, please, tell us whether you remember what this first sentence meant, that sentence confront the strategy of exhaustion with a strategy of offensive initiative. Do you recall what this entry refers to in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entry refers to what Mr. Milosevic said when in analysing the situation he drew a conclusion that the Croats, because of strong logistical, diplomatic, and other support on the one hand, and the Muslim or Bosniak side in Bosnia because of superior numbers, they are counting on the strategy of exhaustion, of attrition due to or through war means or war -- state war stresses, and that such strategy should be countered with a strategy of diplomatic, not military offensive, meaning diplomatic initiatives. And then also discusses what had always been subject to speculation, which I could not really dwell on, and that would be the relationship of US and German strategies in the Balkans, which is something above my head. I would rather refrain from discussing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to take sides or to express your statement, but I'm asking you whether you recall what Milosevic's position was on this issue during that conversation? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- Mr. Milosevic expressed his conclusions based on an analysis of the relationship between the US and Germany, and this entry refers to his estimate or assessment that the US would notice that their policy in the Balkans was pro-German.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the opinion and attitude of Milosevic of the time in relation to the German policies in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His assessment was that after the unification of Germany, Germany wanted to define its place in Europe and that the easiest way for Germany to flex its muscles was the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the next page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, let me skip something. What I'm after would be row 4. RSK, what your memory tells us about this entry, this sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what had transpired beforehand, Mr. Milosevic stated that the Republic of Serbian Krajina should be defended with the help of the RS and the Republic of Serbia, and the FRY, that was the gists of his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you believe at the time while he was uttering those words that this help of the RS and FRY would materialise in terms of aiding the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My most frank answer would be I wanted to believe. I'm not sure whether you are satisfied with this answer or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment. You spoke about the position of General Perisic within the VJ and its any possible involvement in the conflicts and that was on Thursday. Let me ask you again, initially we discussed your knowledge about the position of Mr. Perisic within the VJ and the attitude of the FRY towards the war. Did you believe when this sentence was uttered that the VJ would get embroiled into the conflict in order to defend the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Object to that, Your Honour. The question has already been asked and answered, frankly. At page 64, line 5, he says "I wanted to believe it."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was his answer concerning what was stated as support on the part of the FRY. My question is whether he believed that the VJ could help the defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, a distinction is being drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I withdraw my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, General, you understood my question. Did you at the time believe that the VJ could help the defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the VJ could in a very limited scope defend -- to help the defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you expound on what you term "limited scope," what was that limited scope of aid or assistance to the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VJ as per the then assessment of the Main Staff of the SVK while limited by two important factors had a political decision been taken to -- for them to help the defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The first was the disastrous equipment and material, financial state of affairs in the VJ. And the second, the non-existence of political will among the people in Serbia to take part in war. That was brought about the very dire economic situation in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we may revisit this issue through the entry. The next line says: "Concept of defence and the army. Have the army for defence and to fight the enemy in case of German invasion." I will skip the next sentence. Can you follow or shall I read it out? "The concept of a professional army does not suit us, not even the concept of a Serbian army..." Then: "The concept of ONO must not be discarded because it is proven. It is based," and then there are some other entries. First of my question would be what is the concept of ONO; what does this acronym stand for?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is precisely why I asked this question because we have a different translation here. And then it says number 1, "It can be applied to our own country." Number 2, "The people must be prepared to fight." And number 3, "The army must be prepared to fight even under exacerbated war conditions." And after that it says: "There can only be one army." This last sentence, to whom does it refer? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, you have here the concept of All People's Defence as a concept of Defence for the FRY [as interpreted]. This concept was as much based on expert and military premises as it was based on idealogical premises. In other words, they believed that all people's and ethnic groups led by the communist forces would defend our country to the last drop of blood if it were to be attacked from the outside. So this is an idealogically painted concept. Now, Mr. Milosevic is trying here to revive it in a certain manner. I didn't understand that at the time because the conditions have changed completely in the meantime. However, this contains an answer to your question about the meaning, there can be only one army. This is a comment that actually means what is a new aspect that even in his view was not feasible within the concept of the All People's Defence. In the All People's Defence concept, there were two components of armed forces, the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, and that led to a plethora of problems. Now, when referring to the concept of All People's Defence, he is saying that in spite of everything, there can only be one army. There could not be two armies in a single country as was the case before the war, and I'm talking about the JNA and the Territorial Defence, because that undermines the most significant principles on which an army is founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just correct the transcript. On page 66, in line 10, the witness said SFRY when he talked about this concept of defence. Your Honours, I would like to propose that we adjourn for today because we are going to deal next with the statements of Mr. Perisic and his contributions, and anyway, Mr. Saxon asked for us to adjourn earlier. I see that the Judge has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: You said exacerbated war conditions in your question. Exacerbated war conditions, point number 3. And I have here in my English version "unclear war conditions." You have the original there, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the interpreters in the booth and General Novakovic, I'm going to read this entry once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Should -- perhaps Mr. Novakovic not read that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps that's best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I fully agree. General, please look at item 3 and can you please read it and help us with this handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The army must be prepared to fight under intensified war conditions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, you were saying you would want us to stop now because?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Mr. Saxon would like to address the Chamber, and I think that the witness can be excused because it has to do with housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Novakovic, you are excused. You may stand down now. We are not done with you. You are still in the witness-stand, but you are excused for the day. Once again, you may not discuss the case with anybody until you are finally excused from further testifying. Have a good rest tonight, we'll see you tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukic, before I hand over to Mr. Saxon, Defence Exhibit 03384D has not been tendered. I don't know what you intend doing with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have to go through this document with the witness tomorrow and after that I will make a submission. Are you referring to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have two matters to raise this evening with the Trial Chamber. First of all, is related to a particular exhibit, an exhibit that has been MFI'd as P2894. Your Honours will recall that during the testimony of General Miodrag Simic during the cross-examination, the Trial Chamber admitted a number of documents related to the so-called Drina plan for the purposes of impeachment only. And, Your Honours, in Exhibit P2894 as it was admitted and as it presently resides on e-court, there are several pages, as you can see in my hand, that appear to have information redacted, they are here in black. But subsequent to the testimony of General Simic, the Prosecution re-examined the original copy of this material and discovered that actually in the original version, and what is now a better scanned version, those items that appear in black, that appear to be redacted are simply highlighted in read highlighting and there is information that is visible below the highlighting. I've brought this to Defence counsel's attention and they have no objection that this more readable version of the exhibit be uploaded into e-court, but I seek leave of the Trial Chamber before we ask the Registrar to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree and I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It may be uploaded, Mr. Saxon. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Secondly, Your Honour, tomorrow will be, officially anyway, my last day of work at this Tribunal. I don't believe you will be seeing me in this courtroom again, and so I would like to express to the Trial Chamber my appreciation for having the privilege of appearing before you during this past two years. Also, I'd like to express my great regard for my colleagues on the Defence side of the bar for their diligence and skill in defending General Perisic during the course of this trial. I wish them the best of luck in the final months of this case, and I certainly wish Your Honours the best of luck in the process of completing your judgement. So all I can say is thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. I think I'm speaking on behalf of the Chamber when I say that the Chamber regrets that you are leaving us in the middle of the job before we are finished it. We -- the Chamber is less the luckier for the lack of your wisdom that you have contributed to this case and we hope, however, that the remaining team will still be able to take us through to the end of the case. Whatever you are going to be doing in the future, may you have blessings and best of luck in your future endeavours and future career and you will be sorely missed, and your contribution to this case will be sorely missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Your Honour, and I have absolutely no doubt that may colleagues on the Prosecution team will bring this case to a full and successful conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Is that it? Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Defence team, I would just like to say a few words. According to the common practice, the relationship between Defence and team resembles a relationship between a cat and a dog; however, it was my great pleasure to have on the opposite side Mr. Saxon, and I appreciate the professional attitude that he exercised in his work. Although he was our opponent, he told me that he was contemplating going into education system and I was greatly impressed by that, and I would like to wish him on behalf of all of us who were greatly beneficial in learning so much in this kind of cross fertilisation in the courtroom. I hope that what he learned will impart to his future students, and I really wish him all the success in his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Congratulations on your new appointment, Mr. Saxon. I guess that brings us to the end of the day's proceedings. Court adjourned to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom II.
